story.title: YouTube is reportedly preparing to settle social media addiction claims for $3 billion

facts.text: Meta, Snap, TikTok and YouTube settled an earlier lawsuit with a school district in Kentucky in May, in which YouTube agreed to pay slightly more than $2 million.
The video platform was also found negligent in a personal-injury lawsuit in Los Angeles in March and agreed to settle a separate personal-injury lawsuit in June .
The settlement "will likely take a few months to officially finalize" and is contingent on a majority of districts agreeing.
The deal will reportedly also include "additional product safeguards for teens."
Engadget has asked YouTube to comment on the school district settlement.

Like Meta, Snap and TikTok, YouTube is facing a growing number of lawsuits alleging that its platform is designed to be addictive, and that it knew using it could produce negative outcomes for younger users.

YouTube and many other Google products are heavily used in classrooms, so reaching a settlement would allow the company to avoid drawn-out legal battles during what's already a contentious moment between Google and schools .
YouTube is preparing to pay $3 billion to thousands of school districts to settle claims that its “addictive design” harmed kids, according to Bloomberg.
In March, both YouTube and Meta were found negligent in a separate legal battle over social media addiction.
As part of the agreement, Meta will only shell out the remaining $5.3 billion of its $17.1 billion settlement if YouTube and TikTok roll out similar changes and pay matching amounts.
Sources tell the publication that YouTube reached the agreement “in principle,” and that the deal would also include new safeguards for teens.
The settlement would allow Google to avoid a wave of lawsuits filed by US school districts that accuse YouTube, Meta, Snap, and TikTok of negatively impacting the mental health of teen users.

The Google-owned video platform could pay about $3 billion to thousands of school districts that accuse it of designing an addictive service that harmed students’ mental health, a Bloomberg report claimed, citing people familiar with the matter.

The proposed agreement also includes additional safeguards for teenagers who use YouTube.​The agreement depends on a majority of the districts signing on and could take several months to finalise, the report claims.

They say the companies knew about the risks to young users and failed to change their products to reduce those risks.​The cases bring together claims from multiple school districts so that common issues can be handled before trial, while each district’s case is decided separately.
A settlement would allow YouTube to resolve claims from participating districts.

Thousands of individual personal injury lawsuits against the company remain active.​What happened in the Kentucky case​The first school district case set to go to trial involved Breathitt County, Kentucky, a district with fewer than 2,000 students.

YouTube, Meta, Snap and TikTok settled with the district for a combined $27 million about a month before the trial was due to begin.​YouTube agreed to pay slightly more than $2 million and provide training programs to the district, according to documents released under Kentucky’s open records law.

Google spokesperson José Castaneda and the plaintiffs’ attorneys co-leading the federal school district cases have yet to comment.​Why school districts sued YouTubeThe districts allege that features such as autoplay and endless scrolling encourage students to spend more time on social media.
YouTube has reached a preliminary settlement with US schools.
The districts are seeking reimbursement for expenses they say stem from social media addiction, including the cost of expanding counselling and mental health services for students.
In March 2026, a Los Angeles jury awarded $6 million in an addiction case against Meta and YouTube.
The decision is documented in Meta’s filing and the court verdict .
Both companies challenged the ruling, which Cryptopolitan covered .
The agreement still needs several approvals before it can move forward.
A majority of the school districts involved in the lawsuits must accept YouTube’s proposed settlement, which includes about $3 billion in compensation and additional safeguards for teenagers.
Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers must then approve the agreement.
They claim that this has necessitated schools to increase their spending on mental health services and to enforce phone restrictions.
If this amount is maintained throughout the year, the annual revenue would be around $44.8 billion.
This agreement is currently in its preliminary stage.
Limiting YouTube use during school hours is not straightforward because teachers also rely on the platform for lessons.
Students, however, do not always use it for educational purposes.
The federal lawsuit, case 22-md-03047-YGR , focuses on allegations that how YouTube was designed hurts students’ mental health.
YouTube is not alone in facing these allegations.

Thousands of lawsuits filed by individuals, school districts and government agencies accuse social media companies, including Meta, TikTok and Snap, of designing platforms that encourage addictive behavior among young people.
According to the American Psychological Association , these cases focus on features such as autoplay and infinite scrolling, rather than the content users post.
The settlement could have consequences beyond the money YouTube pays.
Changes to autoplay and personalized recommendations could affect how viewers discover videos, potentially reducing advertising opportunities for content creators.
Johns Hopkins researcher Johannes Thrul estimates that social media addiction affects roughly 5% of people worldwide.
Another trial involving the Tucson school district and other social media platforms is scheduled for February 2027.
